cities.base: The Lower East Side or the top of Chinatown, around Orchard and Delancey. You are walking distance from Katz's, the Tenement Museum and the Bowery, the F, J and M put you anywhere, and it is far livel
cities.name: Lower Manhattan

cities.base: Hell's Kitchen between 44th and 55th, west of Eighth Avenue. Close enough to walk to the theatres, MoMA and Grand Central, one block from a subway line that goes everywhere, and you eat on Ninth Avenu
cities.name: Midtown

cities.base: Between 72nd and 86th, Columbus to West End. Central Park at the end of the block, the Natural History Museum and Zabar's within ten minutes, the 1, 2, 3, B and C all running, and the Met is a twenty
cities.name: Upper West Side

cities.base: Williamsburg around Bedford and North 6th, or Dumbo if you want the waterfront. Williamsburg has the food and the bars and a one-stop L train to 14th Street; Dumbo is prettier, quieter and dead after
cities.name: Brooklyn (Williamsburg and Dumbo)

cities.base: Central Harlem between 125th and 135th, near Lenox or Frederick Douglass. Roughly half the nightly rate of Midtown, the 2 and 3 express trains reach Times Square in about fifteen minutes, and the top
cities.name: Harlem

cities.base: Astoria around 30th Avenue or Broadway, on the N and W. The cheapest beds of the six bases, Greek and Egyptian and Bangladeshi food on the same block, twenty minutes to Midtown, and the 7 train from Q
cities.name: Queens (Astoria)

places.name: Katz's Delicatessen
places.note: Take the ticket at the door, go to the cutters at the counter rather than the waiter section, tip the cutter a dollar and you get a taste while he works. Open 24 hours from Friday morning through Sunday night. The pastrami sandwich is $28.95.

places.name: Russ & Daughters
places.note: The Houston Street shop is a counter, not a restaurant: take a number, order a sable and cream cheese on a bialy, eat it on the street. The sit-down cafe is around the corner on Orchard and takes reservations.

places.name: Nom Wah Tea Parlor
places.note: Dim sum made to order off a paper checklist, not off carts, on the bend of Doyers Street. The egg roll is the thing they are actually famous for.

places.name: Tenement Museum
places.note: Access is by guided tour only and the good ones sell out a week ahead, so book a specific apartment tour before you fly. Tours leave from the visitor centre at 103 Orchard, not from the tenement itself.

places.name: The 9/11 Memorial pools
places.note: Free, open air, and much better after dark when the water is lit and the crowd thins. The names on the parapet are grouped by where people were that morning, not alphabetically.

places.name: 9/11 Memorial Museum
places.note: Heavy going and honest about it; ninety minutes is the minimum and some people need to leave early. Closed Tuesdays apart from a handful of announced dates, and free Monday evenings from 17:30 if you book the moment tickets drop.

places.name: The Staten Island Ferry
places.note: Free, runs all night, and passes the Statue of Liberty close enough that paying for the Liberty Island boat is optional. Stand on the right side going out, get off at St George and walk straight back on.

places.name: The Brooklyn Bridge on foot
places.note: Walk it Brooklyn to Manhattan for the skyline, or do it Manhattan side before 08:00 which is the only hour it is not shoulder to shoulder. The bike lane is now separate, so nobody will shout at you.

places.name: Essex Market
places.note: The old market moved across Delancey into a new building and kept most of its Puerto Rican and Dominican stalls alongside the newer ones. Cheaper lunch than anything else on this block.

places.name: Scarr's Pizza
places.note: They mill their own flour in the basement and the slice is worth the wait, which on a Friday night runs to forty minutes. Go at 15:00 on a weekday and walk straight in.

places.name: Great N.Y. Noodletown
places.note: Salt baked squid, roast baby pig over rice, fluorescent lighting and no ceremony at all. It stays open past midnight, which is why cooks eat here after service.

places.name: African Burial Ground National Monument
places.note: Fifteen thousand graves found under a federal building site in 1991, with a small free visitor centre that explains slavery in colonial New York better than anywhere else in the city. Closed Sundays and Mondays.

places.name: The Mulberry Street restaurants
places.note: Three blocks of sidewalk hosts waving menus at tourists, and the food is priced for people who will not come back. Chinatown starts one street over and is better in every way.

places.name: Grand Central Terminal
places.note: Free, open from before dawn until after midnight, and the ceiling is a painted sky with the constellations reversed. Go down to the Whispering Gallery outside the Oyster Bar and stand in diagonal corners.

places.name: The Rose Main Reading Room, New York Public Library
places.note: Two blocks long and free, but visitors only get the visiting hour, 10:00 to 11:00 with last entry at 10:50, and the building is closed Mondays. There is no visiting hour on Sunday, so make it a weekday or Saturday morning, and sign up for the free tour.

places.name: MoMA
places.note: Open every day of the week, which makes it the fix for a Wednesday when the Met is shut. Start on floor 5 and work down, and expect a scrum in front of Starry Night. Fridays it stays open to 20:30.

places.name: The Morgan Library & Museum
places.note: Pierpont Morgan's private study and three-storey library, plus a Gutenberg Bible and whatever manuscript show is up. Closed Mondays, open until 20:00 on Fridays.

places.name: Keens Steakhouse
places.note: Open since 1885 with ninety thousand clay pipes on the ceiling. Order the mutton chop, which is the only thing here nobody else in the city does, and book weeks out.

places.name: Los Tacos No. 1
places.note: Standing room only, adobada off the trompo, and the one place within five blocks of Times Square worth eating in. Order the nopal taco too.

places.name: Grand Central Oyster Bar
places.note: Sit at the counter under the Guastavino tiles, order oysters and the pan roast, ignore the dining room. Closed Sundays.

places.name: Top of the Rock
places.note: If you insist on one deck, this is the one, because it is the only one with the Empire State Building in the view. Book the slot about forty minutes before sunset. General admission is 34 to 40 dollars and last entry is 22:10.

places.name: SUMMIT One Vanderbilt
places.note: Mirrored rooms, a glass lift and a queue for photographs, at a higher price than any other deck. You are paying for the mirrors, not the view, and the view is worse than Top of the Rock.

places.name: Times Square
places.note: Advertising boards, costumed characters working for tips and the slowest pavement in North America. Walk through it once on the way somewhere if you must, then leave.

places.name: Ninth Avenue, Hell's Kitchen
places.note: Twenty blocks of Thai, Ethiopian, Mexican and old Irish bars, five minutes west of the theatres and priced for people who live there. This is where you eat before a show, not Restaurant Row.

places.name: St. Patrick's Cathedral
places.note: Free, open all day, and a genuinely quiet twenty minutes in the loudest part of the city. The Lady Chapel behind the altar is the part most people walk past.

places.name: 32nd Street, Koreatown
places.note: One block, stacked three floors deep with barbecue, soft tofu and 24-hour seolleongtang. Gammeeok and Her Name Is Han are the two to aim at; most of the block runs very late.

places.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
places.note: Closed Wednesdays, which catches people out more than any other fact in this city. Out-of-state visitors pay the full 30 dollars; the ticket also covers the Cloisters the same day. Open to 21:00 on Fridays and Saturdays.

places.name: American Museum of Natural History
places.note: Open every day. Out-of-state admission is 37 dollars and the Gilder Center extension is the reason to go even if you think you have outgrown dinosaurs.

places.name: The Frick Collection
places.note: Back in the mansion after the renovation, with the upstairs family rooms open for the first time. Closed Tuesdays, pay what you wish on Wednesday afternoons from 13:30, and children under ten are not admitted.

places.name: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
places.note: Take the lift to the top and walk down the ramp, which is what Wright intended. Open seven days now, with pay what you wish Tuesdays and Sundays from 16:00.

places.name: Neue Galerie and Cafe Sabarsky
places.note: Klimt's gold portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer, and a Viennese cafe downstairs that is worth the visit on its own. Closed Tuesdays, and note the galleries are shut for works until 12 November 2026 while the cafe reopens on 1 October.

places.name: The Ramble, Central Park
places.note: Thirty-six acres of deliberately confusing woodland paths in the middle of the park, and the best bird-watching in Manhattan during the May and September migrations. You will get lost; that is the design.

places.name: Bethesda Terrace and the Mall
places.note: The elm tunnel down the Mall and the tiled arcade under the terrace, where there is usually someone singing because the acoustics do the work. Crowded from 11:00 onwards on any decent weekend.

places.name: Barney Greengrass
places.note: The Sturgeon King since 1908, formica tables, eggs scrambled with onions and lox. Closed Mondays and it shuts by mid-afternoon, so this is a breakfast plan or nothing.

places.name: Zabar's
places.note: A grocery that functions as a neighbourhood institution: coffee, smoked fish, cheese counter, and a cafe next door where a sandwich costs a third of what the museum cafes charge.

places.name: Levain Bakery
places.note: A six-ounce cookie that is deliberately underbaked in the middle. One is enough for two people and the queue moves faster than it looks.

places.name: Gray's Papaya
places.note: Two hot dogs and a papaya drink, standing up, at any hour of the day or night. It is the cheapest honest meal on the Upper West Side.

places.name: The Met Cloisters
places.note: Four French monastery cloisters rebuilt above the Hudson in Fort Tryon Park, with the unicorn tapestries. Closed Wednesdays like the main Met, and your Met ticket covers it the same day.

places.name: Brooklyn Bridge Park and the Dumbo waterfront
places.note: Piers 1 to 6 along the East River with the whole Manhattan skyline facing you. Pier 1 at sunset is the view; the cobbled street with the bridge framed between warehouses is Washington Street and it is a photo queue.

places.name: Brooklyn Museum
places.note: Egyptian collection, American period rooms and Judy Chicago's Dinner Party, with a fraction of the Met's crowd. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays.

places.name: Prospect Park Long Meadow
places.note: Olmsted and Vaux built this after Central Park and thought it was the better one. A mile of open meadow, no skyline, and mostly people who live within ten blocks.

places.name: Peter Luger Steak House
places.note: Porterhouse for two, creamed spinach, waiters who have worked there thirty years and will not pretend to like you. No credit cards at all: cash, US debit or a Luger card, and book a month ahead.

places.name: L'Industrie Pizzeria
places.note: Slice shop on South 2nd Street, burrata slice, twenty-minute line most of the day. Go at opening or after 21:00.

places.name: Smorgasburg Williamsburg
places.note: Seventy-odd food stalls outdoors at Marsha P. Johnson State Park on Kent Avenue, Saturdays 11:00 to 18:00 only. The Prospect Park edition runs Sundays; both are seasonal and stop for the winter.

places.name: The Williamsburg Bridge on foot
places.note: Twenty-five minutes across from Bedford Avenue to Delancey Street, with the J and M trains running beside you at eye level. Nobody walks it, which is the point.

places.name: Maison Premiere
places.note: Absinthe, a long marble oyster bar and a back garden. Happy hour oysters until 19:00 on weekdays are the cheapest good oysters in Brooklyn.

places.name: Tacos El Bronco
places.note: Fifth Avenue in Sunset Park is thirty blocks of Mexican and Chinese cooking and this is the anchor: al pastor off the spit, cabeza, a truck out front and a dining room behind it.

places.name: Green-Wood Cemetery
places.note: 478 acres of Victorian funerary landscape on the ridge above the harbour, free to walk into, with a monk parakeet colony in the Gothic gate. Battle Hill is the highest natural point in Brooklyn.

places.name: Juliana's Pizza
places.note: Patsy Grimaldi came back and opened this next door to the place that took his name. Coal oven, same pizza, shorter line.

places.name: Grimaldi's
places.note: The queue on Front Street is forty minutes long and the pizza it leads to is worse than the one next door at Juliana's, which the original owner opened after selling the name.

places.name: Lucali
places.note: One room, candles, no menu beyond pizza and calzone, bring your own wine. You put your name down when the door opens around 17:00 and are told to come back in three hours; closed Tuesdays.

places.name: The Studio Museum in Harlem
places.note: Reopened in its new Adjaye-designed building on 125th Street after years in temporary space. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays, pay what you can, free on Sundays, open to 21:00 on Fridays.

places.name: Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture
places.note: A research library of the African diaspora with free exhibition galleries and Langston Hughes's ashes under the lobby floor. Closed Sundays and hours shift with the library schedule, so check the day before.

places.name: Sylvia's
places.note: Open on Lenox Avenue since 1962 and a James Beard America's Classic. Smothered chicken, collards, cornbread; the Sunday gospel brunch is the busy shift and needs a booking.

places.name: Red Rooster Harlem
places.note: Marcus Samuelsson's room on Lenox, open every day, with live music downstairs at Ginny's most nights. Pricier and more polished than the rest of this list, and it knows it.

places.name: Charles Pan-Fried Chicken
places.note: Cast iron, small kitchen, chicken that takes twenty minutes because it is actually being fried to order. Hours are short and change, so call before you walk up there.

places.name: Dinosaur Bar-B-Que
places.note: A big loud barbecue room under the viaduct on 125th near the river, ribs and brisket, and no pretence that it is a New York dish. Good for a group and for a late lunch.

places.name: Hamilton Grange National Memorial
places.note: Alexander Hamilton's country house, moved twice and now restored in St Nicholas Park. Free, ranger-led, and open Wednesday to Sunday only.

places.name: Mount Morris Park historic district
places.note: Brownstone blocks around Marcus Garvey Park, with the 1856 cast iron fire watchtower at the top of the rock. Climb the steps for a flat view straight down Fifth Avenue.

places.name: Sunday service at Abyssinian Baptist Church
places.note: A working congregation, not a show: dress properly, arrive by 10:00 for the 11:00 service, stay for the whole thing or do not go. Sundays only, and the tourist line is separate from the members' door.

places.name: The Apollo Theater
places.note: The Historic Theater on 125th is closed for renovation and expected back in late 2026, so check before you plan a night around it. Programming has moved to the Apollo Stages at the Victoria two doors down.

places.name: Bill's Place
places.note: A speakeasy-sized jazz room in a 133rd Street brownstone where Billie Holiday was discovered, Friday and Saturday sets only, bring your own bottle. Reserve by phone, twenty seats.

places.name: The Harlem Meer and the North Woods
places.note: The top end of Central Park: a lake people fish in, a ravine with a waterfall, and almost no tourists above 100th Street. Ten minutes on foot from the 2 and 3 at 110th.

places.name: Museum of the Moving Image
places.note: Built into the old Astoria Studios lot, with the Jim Henson collection and a working screening programme. Open Thursday to Sunday only, and free on Thursday afternoons from 14:00.

places.name: The Noguchi Museum
places.note: Isamu Noguchi's own studio and stone garden, converted by him. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays; free the first Friday of the month.

places.name: Socrates Sculpture Park
places.note: A reclaimed landfill on the East River turned into an outdoor sculpture space, free, five minutes' walk from the Noguchi. The Manhattan view across the water is the second reason to go.

places.name: Taverna Kyclades
places.note: Grilled whole fish, octopus and free semolina cake, on Ditmars near the end of the N train. They take bookings now, which they did not for thirty years, and you should use that.

places.name: Astoria Seafood
places.note: You pick raw fish off ice by the pound, pay at the counter, and they cook it for a small charge. Cash preferred, bring your own wine, no atmosphere whatsoever and that is fine.

places.name: Astoria Park and the Hell Gate Bridge
places.note: Under two enormous bridges on the East River, with the largest and oldest public pool in the city. The best free skyline view in Queens, and locals only after dark.

places.name: Nan Xiang Xiao Long Bao
places.note: Soup dumplings, done properly, in a full-size restaurant on Prince Street rather than a food-court stall. Expect a wait at weekend lunch and take the number.

places.name: New World Mall food court
places.note: A basement of about thirty regional Chinese stalls under Roosevelt Avenue: Xi'an hand-pulled noodles, Chengdu skewers, Lanzhou beef noodle soup. Bring cash and point.

places.name: Joe's Steam Rice Roll
places.note: Cheung fun steamed to order on cloth, which almost nobody does any more, for about eight dollars. Eat it standing; there are four stools.

places.name: Louis Armstrong House Museum
places.note: The modest Corona house Armstrong lived in until he died, kept exactly as it was, with his home tape recordings. Open Thursday to Saturday only, hourly tours from 11:00 to 15:00.

places.name: Queens Museum and the Unisphere
places.note: The Panorama of the City of New York, a 9,335 square foot model of all five boroughs built for the 1964 World's Fair. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays, pay what you wish, and the Unisphere is outside the door.

places.name: Birria-Landia
places.note: A truck under the 7 train at 78th Street doing birria tacos and consomme. Roosevelt Avenue for thirty blocks either side is Colombian, Ecuadorian, Mexican and Tibetan food at truck prices.

places.name: Empire State Building
places.note: Finished in April 1931 and 1,454 feet to the tip; the open-air 86th floor deck is from $46 and adding the 102nd is from $81. Book a slot ahead because sunset sells out, go on a weekday between 09:00 and 10:30, and the doors close at 22:00.

places.name: Bryant Park
places.note: Nine and a half free acres beside the library, opened in 1847 as Reservoir Square and home to the 1853 Crystal Palace until it burned in 1858. Hours vary, check; it is the place to sit down between the library and Grand Central.

places.name: St Paul's Chapel
places.note: Built 1764 to 1766, the oldest church building left in Manhattan; Washington prayed here on inauguration day in 1789, and after 9/11 it was a rest stop for recovery workers for nine months. See the pew plaque and the 9/11 exhibit. Hours vary, check, and check the price.

places.name: Federal Hall National Memorial
places.note: The 1842 Greek Revival hall stands where the first US Capitol did: Washington took the oath on its balcony on 30 Apr 1789 and Congress proposed the Bill of Rights here. Free, but the open days disagree between sources, so hours vary, check (212-825-6990).

places.name: Fraunces Tavern Museum
places.note: Built in 1719; in the Long Room Washington said goodbye to his officers on 4 Dec 1783, and that room is the reason to come. $10, open daily 12:00 to 17:00, no booking needed; a weekday afternoon is quietest. A new exhibit, Martha, opens 16 Nov 2026.

places.name: Statue of Liberty
places.note: Dedicated 28 Oct 1886: Bartholdi's statue on Eiffel's frame and Hunt's pedestal. The $26 ferry from Castle Clinton, the only authorised ticket office, also stops at Ellis Island; pedestal and crown are booked ahead. Take the first boat and see the pedestal museum. Hours vary, check.
places.neighborhood: Liberty Island, ferry from Battery Park

places.name: Ellis Island National Museum of Immigration
places.note: About 12 million immigrants came through between 1892 and 1954; the 1900 main building has been the museum since 1990. Free to enter, but you need the $26 Statue ferry, so do both on one ticket. The south side hospital is by guided tour only. Hours vary, check.
places.neighborhood: Ellis Island, same ferry as the Statue

places.name: Intrepid Museum
places.note: A carrier commissioned in 1943, a museum since 1982, with the Space Shuttle Enterprise on the flight deck, a Concorde and the submarine Growler alongside. $38; 10:00 to 17:00 weekdays, to 18:00 at weekends, but confirm on the museum's own page. Give it two and a half hours.

places.name: New-York Historical
places.note: Founded in 1804, the city's oldest museum: one of the biggest Tiffany lamp collections, Hudson River School paintings and Washington relics. Closed Mondays, open to 20:00 on Fridays. Check the price on nyhistory.org; it was not confirmed in dollars.

places.name: The Dakota
places.note: Henry Hardenbergh's 1884 block, the oldest surviving luxury apartment building in the city, and where John Lennon was shot on 8 Dec 1980. Exterior only, it is a private co-op; free to look, then cross to Strawberry Fields.

places.name: Strawberry Fields
places.note: Yoko Ono's teardrop garden for Lennon, with the black and white Imagine mosaic; it is a quiet zone and free. Go early in the morning, and expect crowds around 9 Oct and 8 Dec.

places.name: General Grant National Memorial (Grant's Tomb)
places.note: Finished in 1897 on Grant's 75th birthday, the biggest mausoleum in North America; walk round the mosaic bench outside. Wednesday to Sunday 10:00 to 16:00, closed on the big holidays; visitors say it is free, but check the price on the NPS page.

places.name: Riverside Church
places.note: Rockefeller Jr. paid for this Neo-Gothic church, built 1927 to 1930, long a pulpit for social justice; come for the stained glass and the bells. Listed 09:00 to 17:00 daily, next to Grant's Tomb; check the price and the hours before you go.

places.name: Brooklyn Heights Promenade
places.note: A 557 m walkway built over the expressway after the war, with the Statue of Liberty, the Brooklyn Bridge and Lower Manhattan straight across; free and always open. Come at sunrise or the last hour of light.

places.name: Grand Army Plaza and Soldiers' and Sailors' Arch
places.note: Calvert Vaux's oval plaza from the 1860s at the top of Prospect Park, with the arch to the Union forces of the Civil War. Free and open; take it on the way to the Brooklyn Museum.

places.name: Domino Park
places.note: Opened in 2018 on the old Domino Sugar refinery site, with salvaged machinery and four syrup tanks along the Artifact Walk and Manhattan across the river. Free, 06:00 to 23:00, and right in the Williamsburg bed.

places.name: New York Transit Museum
places.note: Down in the 1936 Court Street station, shut to passengers in 1946, with vintage subway cars on live track. $15; Wednesday to Sunday 10:00 to 16:00. Book online, tickets release three weeks ahead and walk-ups are limited.

places.name: Weeksville Heritage Center
places.note: Land bought in 1838 by James Weeks, a freed Black stevedore, became one of the largest free Black towns before the Civil War. The centre is free; the Hunterfly Road Houses tour is $10 and must be booked 24 hours ahead. Weekdays from 10:00, Saturday from 11:00.

places.name: Plymouth Church
places.note: Henry Ward Beecher's church from 1847, a stop on the Underground Railroad, where he held mock slave auctions to buy people free; Lincoln came on 26 Feb 1860. A short walk from the Promenade. Hours vary, check the tour schedule and the price.

places.name: Old Stone House
places.note: A 1930s rebuild of the c.1699 farmhouse where the Maryland 400 held off the British on 27 Aug 1776 so the army could escape across Gowanus Creek. Listed Friday to Sunday 12:00 to 16:00; check the price and the hours.

places.name: BLDG 92 at the Brooklyn Navy Yard
places.note: The Navy Yard's story from 1801: the Monitor was commissioned here in 1862, the Arizona launched in 1915, and 75,000 worked here at the WWII peak. Free by visitors' accounts; listed Thursday to Sunday 11:00 to 17:00, so check before you go.

places.name: Morris-Jumel Mansion
places.note: Built in 1765, the oldest house in Manhattan: Washington's HQ in Sep 1776, and Aaron Burr married Eliza Jumel in its parlour in 1833. Temporarily closed for tours, so see the outside and the park (10:00 to 17:00); check the price and reopening before you go.

places.name: Sylvan Terrace
places.note: The 1765 carriage drive to the Morris-Jumel Mansion, lined since 1882 with 20 matching wooden rowhouses. A free public street, 15 minutes, round the corner from the mansion.

places.name: Cathedral of St. John the Divine
places.note: One of the largest cathedrals in the world, building for over 120 years and still unfinished; look for the stained glass and the two organs. $15 self-guided; Monday to Saturday from 09:30, Sunday from 12:00, to 17:00.

places.name: Strivers' Row (St. Nicholas Historic District)
places.note: David King's model houses of 1891 to 1893, partly by Stanford White; they opened to Black buyers in 1919, hence the name, and Eubie Blake, W. C. Handy and Bojangles Robinson lived here. Free to walk, go in daylight, and look down the rear service alleys.
places.neighborhood: W 138th and 139th St, Adam Clayton Powell Jr. to Frederick D

places.name: Mother African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church
places.note: The congregation was founded in 1796 by Black members of John Street Methodist and was a refuge on the Underground Railroad; the church is George W. Foster Jr.'s of 1923 to 1925. Best seen at a Sunday service; hours vary, check, and donations welcome, check.

places.name: Steinway & Sons Factory
places.note: Follow a piano from raw walnut and spruce to final tuning. Tours have run Tuesday mornings, September to June, booked by phone (718-721-2600), 15 people, no under-16s, lots of stairs; that schedule is old, so check it and the price.

places.name: Kaufman Astoria Studios
places.note: Paramount's 1920 East Coast lot: the Marx Brothers' first two films, Army training films in the war, later Sesame Street and The Cosby Show. Exterior only, free from the street; pair it with the Museum of the Moving Image next door.
places.neighborhood: Astoria, next to the Museum of the Moving Image

places.name: Bohemian Hall and Beer Garden
places.note: Run by a Czech society founded in 1892, the hall dates from 1910 and claims to be the city's oldest beer garden; Havel planted the linden in 2000. Czech beer and bratwurst. Closed Mondays; hours vary, check, and check the price and whether the garden is open in winter.

places.name: Flushing Town Hall
places.note: The 1862 round-arch town hall of Flushing village until 1898, now an arts centre with jazz nights ($10 to $18 when we looked). Nine km from Astoria, so fold it into a Flushing day on the 7 train. Hours vary, check the price and the programme.

places.name: Kingsland Homestead
places.note: A farmhouse of about 1785, moved twice and the Queens Historical Society's museum since 1973. $5, Wednesday, Saturday and Sunday 14:30 to 16:30 on timed tickets booked ahead; pair it with Flushing Town Hall for a Flushing half-day.

places.name: Lewis H. Latimer House Museum
places.note: Home from 1903 to 1928 of Lewis Latimer, Edison's chief draftsman and patent expert, who invented a carbon filament in 1879; renovated in 2024. Friday to Sunday 11:00 to 17:00, but confirm Sunday; self-guided is free, the 45 minute guided tour $15.

outings.why: Three hours in the Met from opening at 10:00, out the back door into Central Park, over the Ramble and Bethesda Terrace, and down to Zabar's or Gray's Papaya. The Met is shut on Wednesdays, so this day cannot be a Wednesday.
outings.name: The Met, then across the park to the West Side
outings.fallback: If it rains, the Met plus the Frick, both indoors and eight blocks apart.

outings.why: Brooklyn Bridge before 08:00 while it is still empty, down into Chinatown for dim sum at Nom Wah, the Tenement Museum tour in the early afternoon, then Katz's or Scarr's and the 9/11 pools after dark. About eight miles of walking on concret
outings.name: Downtown on foot: the bridge, Chinatown and the Lower East Side
outings.fallback: Skip the bridge and start at the Tenement Museum, then Essex Market and the Staten Island Ferry.

outings.why: The 7 train to Main Street, soup dumplings at Nan Xiang and a lap of the New World Mall basement, then two stops back to Flushing Meadows for the Panorama at the Queens Museum and the 1964 World's Fair remains. Queens Museum is closed Monda
outings.name: Flushing for lunch, then the Unisphere
outings.fallback: Stay in Flushing and eat your way down Roosevelt Avenue instead; the museum keeps.

outings.why: Long Meadow in the morning, the Brooklyn Museum for two hours, then the Sunday Smorgasburg at the bottom of the park or the Saturday one on Kent Avenue. The museum is closed Monday and Tuesday and the markets only run at weekends in season,
outings.name: Prospect Park, the Brooklyn Museum and Smorgasburg
outings.season: Smorgasburg runs April to late October; the rest is all year
outings.fallback: Brooklyn Museum and the Botanic Garden next door, both under cover enough to survive a wet day.

outings.why: The 11:00 service at Abyssinian Baptist, in the visitors' line by 10:00 and dressed for church, then Sylvia's or Charles for lunch and a walk round the Mount Morris brownstones. Sundays only, and the Studio Museum is free that day if you wa
outings.name: Uptown Sunday: gospel at Abyssinian, then Harlem lunch
outings.fallback: Skip the service and do the Studio Museum, Schomburg and Hamilton Grange on a weekday instead.

outings.why: The Noguchi Museum and Socrates Sculpture Park are two minutes apart on Vernon Boulevard, then the Museum of the Moving Image, then Astoria Park at sunset and fish at Taverna Kyclades. Noguchi is closed Monday and Tuesday and the Moving Ima
outings.name: Astoria: Noguchi, Socrates, then Greek on Ditmars
outings.fallback: Noguchi and a long lunch on 30th Avenue; drop the sculpture park in bad weather.

outings.why: Pizza at Juliana's, the length of Brooklyn Bridge Park along the water, up onto the Promenade for the skyline as the lights come on, and back over the bridge on foot. Flat, short, and the one evening that is worth planning around the weathe
outings.name: Dumbo and the Brooklyn Heights Promenade at sunset
outings.fallback: The ferry from Dumbo to Wall Street gets the same view sitting down and out of the wind.

outings.why: Three hours in MoMA, which is the one big museum open every day of the week, then Grand Central and the Oyster Bar counter, then Top of the Rock forty minutes before sunset. The Oyster Bar is shut on Sundays.
outings.name: MoMA and Midtown after dark
outings.fallback: MoMA plus the Morgan Library, ten minutes apart, if the sky is white and the deck is pointless.

outings.why: The A train forty minutes north to 190th Street, four rebuilt medieval cloisters and the unicorn tapestries above the Hudson, then the heather garden and lunch on Dyckman Street. Closed Wednesdays, same as the main Met, and the same ticket
outings.name: The Cloisters and Fort Tryon Park
outings.season: All year, best in May and October
outings.fallback: If it is pouring, the galleries alone are two hours and the walk down through the park can wait.

destination.name: New York City
destination.pitch: Six days is enough to stop treating it as a list of landmarks and start using it like a city, which means sleeping in two neighbourhoods rather than one and eating in the outer boroughs.
destination.caveat: Beds are the whole budget: 250 dollars a night is a normal midweek room in Manhattan. The two things that ruin days are the fixed closures (the Met on Wednesdays, the Frick and the Whitney on Tuesdays, the Morgan and the library on Mondays) and the January and February wind off the rivers. Put together for you just now from a live search, so check anything you're pinning the trip on.

because.city: This is the reference case. Nothing else on the list is a city in the same way.
because.food: Flushing, Roosevelt Avenue, Sunset Park and the hundred-year-old Jewish and Italian counters on the Lower East Side, most of it under twenty dollars a head.
because.nature: Central Park, Prospect Park and Green-Wood are real landscape design rather than scenery, and the Ramble in migration season is serious birding, but nobody flies here for nature.
because.culture: The Met, MoMA, the Frick, the Morgan, the Whitney, the Studio Museum and the Brooklyn Museum, plus live jazz in rooms that hold twenty people.
because.adventure: Only in the sense that walking eleven miles and crossing three bridges in a day is a physical undertaking.
because.relaxation: Not what this is. The quietest hours are early mornings in the parks and the Staten Island Ferry at night.
because.exploration: Six bases on one subway map, and the distance between Ditmars Boulevard and Sunset Park is bigger than the distance between most European capitals.
